title: Workers Organize
objective: After this level you can explain why industrial workers struck and formed unions, and what the Triangle fire of 1911 changed.
summary: Workers formed unions to bargain as a group. Homestead (1892) was a defeat, the 1909 shirtwaist strike won gains, and the 1911 Triangle fire led to new safety laws.

cards.headline: In 1911, 146 garment workers died in a fire. Many exits were locked.
cards.body: Why did workers keep organizing and striking in these decades, and what finally changed the rules?

cards.headline: Bargaining as a group
cards.body: A labor union is an association of workers that seeks better pay and conditions by bargaining with employers as a group. Employers didn’t always accept that. In 1892, at Carnegie’s Homestead steel works in Pennsylvania, managers locked out the workers and sent 300 Pinkerton agents to seize the plant. The battle left three Pinkertons and seven strikers dead, and the state militia broke the strike and the union.

cards.headline: The Uprising of the 20,000
cards.body: In November 1909, Clara Lemlich, 23, stood up at a New York meeting and called for a general strike. Thousands of shirtwaist makers, mostly young immigrant women, walked out. The strike lasted over two months and won better pay and shorter hours at many shops. The people sewing the country’s blouses had shown they could shut the shops down.

cards.headline: Locked doors
cards.body: On March 25, 1911, fire broke out at the Triangle Waist Company in New York. The doors were locked or opened inward, and many exits were blocked or broken. 146 garment workers died, mostly young immigrant women.
cards.callout: 146 workers died in the Triangle fire of March 25, 1911

cards.headline: What changed
cards.body: New York set up a Factory Investigating Commission, which led to more than 30 health and safety laws, including fire codes and limits on child labor. One witness to the fire, Frances Perkins, later became US Secretary of Labor. The fire made the case the strikers had been making.

cards.headline: Workers organize: explained
learned: Unions bargain with employers as a group
Homestead (1892) ended with the union broken
Clara Lemlich sparked the 1909 shirtwaist strike
The Triangle fire (1911) led to over 30 safety laws

questions.prompt: How many garment workers died in the Triangle fire of 1911?

options.rationale: That echoes the 1909 strike’s name, not the fire.

questions.explanation: The Triangle fire of March 25, 1911, killed 146 garment workers.

questions.prompt: Why did the Triangle fire lead to new laws, not just grief?

options.label: The factory owners themselves asked for stricter safety rules
options.rationale: The level credits a state commission, not the owners.

options.label: The workers’ union wrote and passed the new laws itself
Locked exits trapped workers, and a state commission pushed reform
Congress quickly banned all garment factories in New York

questions.explanation: Locked doors and blocked exits trapped the workers; New York’s Factory Investigating Commission led to over 30 safety laws.

questions.prompt: In Level 6, Franklin argued the colonies should unite as the Six Nations had. What was the similar idea behind a labor union?

options.label: Each worker should negotiate alone
options.rationale: That is exactly what unions replace.

options.label: Employers should form one company
options.rationale: That’s a monopoly, not a union.

options.label: Workers should elect their employers
options.rationale: Unions bargain; they don’t elect bosses.

options.label: Workers bargain with employers as a group

questions.explanation: Like a union of colonies, a labor union joins workers so they bargain with employers as a group.
